title: "YOLO (You Only Look Once)"
description: "A family of object-detection models designed to predict object locations and classes in one network evaluation."
term: "YOLO (You Only Look Once)"
letter: "Y"
category: "Computer Vision"
difficulty: "Intermediate"
---

## Simple explanation

YOLO is a family of object detectors that predict object locations and labels
from an image in a single model pass, making the approach suitable for
real-time use cases.

## Technical explanation

YOLO refers to a sequence of object-detection architectures rather than one
fixed model. Implementations typically produce box coordinates, class scores,
and confidence-related outputs at one or more feature-map scales. Training
assignments, heads, losses, and post-processing differ across versions;
non-maximum suppression is common but not universal.

## Why it matters in AI engineering

One-pass detectors can offer a useful speed-accuracy trade-off for video,
robotics, and edge deployments. Selection should use a representative
benchmark, including image size, hardware, class imbalance, latency, and
post-processing costs.

## How it works

The model extracts image features and predicts candidate boxes and class
scores. Training compares predictions with labeled objects. At inference,
confidence thresholds and, in many implementations, non-maximum suppression
filter overlapping candidates.

## Practical example

For warehouse package detection, evaluate on images from different cameras,
lighting, and package sizes. Measure per-class precision and recall and actual
throughput on the target device, not only a benchmark score from a different
hardware setup.

## Common misconceptions

- YOLO is a family of models whose details vary by version and implementation.
- “Single pass” does not mean there is no post-processing or that inference
  latency is independent of image size and hardware.
